own_scenes.place: Birmingham, Belfast, Glasgow, Londres y el resto de provincias
own_scenes.desc: Tras el éxito de los Beatles, las cuatro grandes discográficas (EMI, Decca, Pye y Philips) saquearon metódicamente las provincias: firmaban barato y esperaban a ver qué pegaba. Pye, del veterano Louis Benjamin, tenía a los Kinks y a los Searchers y fama de contratos miserables. Los Ugly’s de Birmingham, nacidos del skiffle y curtidos en los clubes alemanes, se distinguían por su conciencia social; la cara B de su tercer single, «A Quiet Explosion» (21 de enero de 1966), con órgano Vox Continental, un riff con eco a lo Delia Derbyshire y un bajo descendente que es la bomba cayendo, desapareció en la sobreproducción del momento, pero es un disco extraño y auténtico que se acerca a la psicodelia. A principios de 1966 las bases del beat y del R&B se llevaron al límite, como bajo una enorme presión: «Keep on Running» de Spencer Davis casa soul y mod pop, los Wheels de Belfast aceleran sin freno en «Bad Little Woman» y los Poets de Glasgow, de Andrew Loog Oldham, desquician el «Baby Don’t You Do It» de Marvin Gaye.

refs.q: The flip side was something quite different. ‘A Quiet Explosion’ begins with the reedy, eerie sound of a Vox Continental organ.
refs.para: The flip side was something quite different. ‘A Quiet Explosion’ begins with the reedy, eerie sound of a Vox Continental organ. It then adds a subtle rolling drum pattern underpinned by a strange, echoing riff reminiscent of the musique concrète electronics pioneered by Delia Derbyshire on 1964’s ‘Dr Who Theme’. ‘That was our bassist John Hustwayte,’ says Gibbons. ‘He played that riff with a plectrum and our producer, Alan A. Freeman, put echo on it. The falling bass run at the end, well, that’s the falling bomb.’
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: Yet it remains a strange, haunting record.
refs.para: Yet it remains a strange, haunting record. It’s not a total success – the lyrics are on occasion garbled – but in its very awkwardness it has the ring of authenticity. It has the sense of thoughtful young men groping towards some understanding of the world in which they live and their place within it: ‘but we must unite and all fight with one cause’. It may not be truly psychedelic, but it pushes forward towards that definition: in its experimental fusion of sound, mood and sense, it is imaginative and holistic.
refs.chapter: Enero: A Quiet Explosion: la CND, la protesta y la conspiración del silencio

refs.q: The stylistic foundations of the beat and R&B booms were pushed to the limit, as if under enormous compression.
refs.para: The stylistic foundations of the beat and R&B booms were pushed to the limit, as if under enormous compression. The week after the release of ‘A Quiet Explosion’, the US trade magazine Cashbox reviewed a 45 by Belfast group the Wheel-A-Ways and gave it a B+: a ‘slow raunchy infectious side’. The Wheels – as they were better known – were contemporaries of Them, the group that Van Morrison fronted, and they also specialised in tough R&B. They’d already covered Them’s ‘Gloria’, but ‘Bad Little Woman’ was something else.

podcast.title: "A Hug for Your Baby" - Merseybeat Pastiche
podcast.body: The demo song "A Hug for Your Baby," written by Dave Davis and recorded by The Bull Weevils (an early iteration of The Kinks), is described as a "Merseybeat pastiche," reflecting a contemporary popular musical style. "The Mursy Beat pastiche, written by Dave Davis, I believe, too."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: "You Still Want Me" - Merseybeat Pastiche
podcast.body: The Kinks' second single, "You Still Want Me," was a "Merseybeat pastiche." This stylistic choice, despite songwriting advice from Larry Page, did not lead to chart success, as the song performed even worse than their debut single. "You still want me, a mercy beat pastiche that didn't even do as well as the group's first record."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 119: "You Really Got Me" by the Kinks

podcast.title: Dominant Scene in Liverpool
podcast.body: Merseybeat was the music scene that produced groups like The Beatles and The Searchers from Liverpool. "The Beatles weren't the only influential band on the mercybeat scene."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 113: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers

podcast.title: Early Live Sound vs. Studio Sound
podcast.body: Many Merseybeat bands, including The Searchers, sounded much more powerful in their earlier live performances than in studio recordings. "Most of the mercybeat bands sounded much more powerful in their earlier live performances than in the studio, and the searchers were no exception."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Influential Single Track - "Needles and Pins"
podcast.body: "Needles and Pins" by The Searchers has a reasonable claim to be the most influential single track from the Merseybeat era due to its invention of Jangle Pop and Folk Rock. "Needles and Pins has a reasonable claim to be the most influential single track from the Mersey Beat era."
